question: Which trophy do Australia and England contest in Test cricket?
explanation: The urn dates from an 1882 mock obituary in the Sporting Times after Australia's first win on English soil, declaring English cricket dead and its ashes taken to Australia.
hook: It began as a newspaper joke obituary for English cricket.

question: Which race is described as the one that stops a nation?
explanation: Run over 3,200 metres at Flemington on the first Tuesday in November, it is a public holiday in metropolitan Melbourne and has been run since 1861.
hook: The only horse race anywhere that comes with its own public holiday.

question: How many players are on the field per team in a game of Australian rules football?
explanation: Rugby union has fifteen, rugby league thirteen and soccer eleven; the eighteen-a-side oval game is played on the largest field of any football code.
hook: Eighteen for Aussie rules, fifteen union, thirteen league, eleven soccer.

question: Which Australian won seven medals at the Tokyo Olympics, a national record?
explanation: Four of the seven were gold, the most by any Australian at a single Games; Ian Thorpe's five career golds came across Sydney and Athens.
hook: Seven medals at one Games — no Australian has ever managed more.

question: How often are the Summer Olympic Games held?
explanation: The four-year gap is called an Olympiad; the 2020 Tokyo Games were postponed to 2021 by the pandemic but kept their original name.
hook: Tokyo 2020 was held in 2021 and still called 2020.

question: Which country has won the most FIFA World Cups?
explanation: Brazil has five titles, Germany and Italy four each, and Brazil is the only nation to have played in every tournament since 1930.
hook: Five titles, and the only country never to miss a World Cup.

question: In tennis, what term describes a score of zero?
explanation: It probably comes from the French l'oeuf, the egg, for the zero's shape; 'duck' is the cricket equivalent, from duck's egg.
hook: Tennis has an egg, cricket has a duck — both shapes of zero.

question: Which Australian tennis tournament is one of the four grand slams?
explanation: Held in Melbourne each January, it joins Roland Garros, Wimbledon and the US Open; it moved to Melbourne Park with a retractable roof in 1988.
hook: Australian Open, French Open, Wimbledon, US Open — January to September.

question: How many holes are played in a standard round of golf?
explanation: St Andrews settled on eighteen in 1764 by combining short holes, and the rest of the golfing world followed the Old Course's lead.
hook: St Andrews merged some holes in 1764 and everyone else copied the number.

question: Which sport uses terms including 'scrum', 'ruck' and 'lineout'?
explanation: Rugby league abolished the lineout and heavily simplified the scrum, which is one of the clearest ways to tell the codes apart on television.
hook: No lineout means you are watching league, not union.

question: Which Australian cricketer is regarded as the greatest batsman of all time?
explanation: His Test average of 99.94 stands far above anyone else's; he needed four runs in his final innings to average 100 and was dismissed for a duck.
hook: Four runs short of a hundred average, out second ball, in his last innings.

question: Which sport is played at Wimbledon?
explanation: The only grand slam still played on grass, it has been contested since 1877 and enforces an all-white clothing rule for players.
hook: The last grass slam, and the only one with a dress code.

question: How many points is a try worth in rugby union?
explanation: A conversion adds two, a penalty or drop goal three; rugby league scores four for a try and two for the conversion.
hook: Union five, league four — the try is worth more in union.

question: Which Australian sporting event is contested annually between NSW and Queensland?
explanation: The rugby league series began in 1980, selecting players by the state where they played their first senior game rather than where they currently live.
hook: You play for where you started, not where you live — that is the whole 'origin' idea.

question: Which country invented the modern game of cricket?
explanation: It developed in south-east England by the sixteenth century, and the MCC at Lord's has held custody of the laws of the game since 1788.
hook: The laws of cricket have lived at Lord's since 1788.

question: How many players are on a basketball team on court at one time?
explanation: James Naismith invented the game in 1891 using peach baskets, with teams of nine; the five-a-side format was standardised by 1897.
hook: It started nine-a-side with actual peach baskets nailed to a balcony.

question: Which Australian golfer won the 2013 US Masters?
explanation: He became the first Australian to win at Augusta, beating Angel Cabrera in a play-off; Greg Norman finished runner-up there three times without winning.
hook: Norman lost the Masters three times; Scott finally broke the drought in 2013.

question: What is a score of three under par on a single golf hole called?
explanation: One under is a birdie, two under an eagle and four under a condor, which has been recorded only a handful of times in history.
hook: Birdie, eagle, albatross, condor — the bird gets bigger as the score gets lower.

question: Which Australian city hosts the AFL Grand Final each year?
explanation: It is contractually locked to the MCG until 2059; the only exceptions were 2020 in Brisbane and 2021 in Perth because of pandemic border closures.
hook: Locked to the MCG until 2059 — only a pandemic has ever moved it.

question: In soccer, how long is a standard match excluding stoppage time?
explanation: Two halves of forty-five minutes; rugby union plays eighty and Australian rules four quarters of twenty minutes plus substantial time on.
hook: Ninety soccer, eighty rugby, and Aussie rules has no fixed length at all.

question: Which Australian won seven world surfing titles?
explanation: She won six consecutively from 1998 and a seventh in 2006; Stephanie Gilmore later won eight, taking the outright record.
hook: Beachley made seven, then Gilmore made eight — both Australian.

question: How many rings are on the Olympic flag?
explanation: They represent the five inhabited continents, and the six colours including the white background were chosen so that every national flag of 1913 contained at least one.
hook: The colours were picked so every nation's flag shared at least one.

question: Which sport features the Tour de France?
explanation: First run in 1903 to sell newspapers, the leader wears yellow because the organising paper L'Auto was printed on yellow newsprint.
hook: The yellow jersey matches the newsprint the sponsoring paper was printed on.

question: Which Australian horse won the 1930 Melbourne Cup and became a national icon?
explanation: He died in California in 1932 in circumstances still debated; his hide is in Melbourne, his skeleton in New Zealand and his heart in Canberra.
hook: His body is split between three museums in two countries.

question: In cricket, what is a score of zero by a batsman called?
explanation: From 'duck's egg' for the round zero; out first ball is a golden duck, and out first ball of the match is a diamond duck.
hook: Golden duck first ball, diamond duck first ball of the innings.

question: Which country hosts the Formula One Monaco Grand Prix?
explanation: Run on public streets since 1929, it is the slowest circuit on the calendar and the hardest to overtake on, yet remains the most prestigious race.
hook: The slowest, narrowest track on the calendar is also the one drivers most want to win.

question: How many players are in a netball team on court?
explanation: Each has a designated position restricting where they may move, and only the goal shooter and goal attack may score.
hook: Seven players, and only two of them are allowed to score.

question: Which Australian swimmer won gold at three consecutive Olympics in the 100m freestyle?
explanation: She won in 1956, 1960 and 1964, and was banned for ten years after allegedly taking a flag from a Tokyo palace, ending her career.
hook: Three golds in a row, then banned for a decade over a flag.

question: What piece of equipment is used to hit the ball in badminton?
explanation: Badminton and tennis use racquets, table tennis uses a paddle or bat, and cricket and baseball use bats; the badminton shuttlecock is the fastest projectile in any racquet sport.
hook: The shuttlecock leaves the racquet faster than any other sporting projectile.

question: How many VFL/AFL premierships have Carlton and Essendon each won?
explanation: They are tied at the top, with Collingwood on fifteen; Carlton's last came in 1995 and Essendon's in 2000, so neither has won this century.
hook: Two clubs tied on sixteen, neither having won since 2000.

question: In which sport would you perform a 'slam dunk'?
explanation: The dunk was banned in US college basketball from 1967 to 1976, a rule widely believed to have been aimed at Kareem Abdul-Jabbar.
hook: College basketball banned it for nine years to slow down one player.

question: Which Australian was known as the 'Rocket' in tennis?
explanation: He is the only player to win the calendar-year grand slam twice, in 1962 and 1969; the Australian Open's main court is named after him.
hook: The only person to win all four slams in one year, twice.

question: How many minutes long is each quarter in an AFL match, excluding time on?
explanation: Time on is added for stoppages, so quarters typically run nearer thirty minutes; the clock stops whenever the ball is out of play.
hook: Twenty minutes on paper, closer to thirty in reality.

question: Which country originated the martial art of judo?
explanation: Jigoro Kano founded it in 1882; taekwondo is Korean, kung fu Chinese and muay thai Thai.
hook: Judo and karate Japanese, taekwondo Korean, kung fu Chinese.

question: What colour jersey does the leader of the Tour de France wear?
explanation: Green marks the points leader, polka dot the best climber and white the best young rider under twenty-six.
hook: Yellow overall, green sprints, polka dot mountains, white for the youngsters.

question: At which Olympics did the women's pole vault make its debut?
explanation: Australia's Tatiana Grigorieva took silver behind Stacy Dragila of the United States; Emma George had held multiple world records through the 1990s.
hook: Women's pole vault only entered the Olympics in 2000, and Australia took silver.

question: Which Australian cricketer took 708 Test wickets?
explanation: His first ball in Ashes cricket, the so-called Ball of the Century to Mike Gatting in 1993, turned a foot and remains the sport's most replayed delivery.
hook: One delivery in 1993 defined a twenty-year career.

question: Which mare won three consecutive Melbourne Cups from 2003 to 2005?
explanation: No other horse has won three; Winx won thirty-three consecutive races but never contested the Cup, and Black Caviar was an unbeaten sprinter.
hook: Three Cups is a record no horse has come close to since.

question: How many Test-playing nations were there when Australia played its first Test in 1877?
explanation: Only Australia and England; South Africa joined in 1889, and the number now stands at twelve after Afghanistan and Ireland were admitted in 2017.
hook: Test cricket began as a two-country sport and took over a century to reach ten.

question: Which sprinter holds the men's 100 metres world record?
explanation: He ran 9.58 seconds in Berlin in 2009, a mark that has stood far longer than any previous 100m record in the electronic timing era.
hook: 9.58 in 2009, and nobody has been within a tenth of it since.

question: Which Australian won the 1983 America's Cup for Australia II?
explanation: He skippered the boat, Alan Bond funded the syndicate and Ben Lexcen designed the winged keel; it ended the New York Yacht Club's 132-year hold on the trophy.
hook: It ended the longest winning streak in the history of sport — 132 years.

question: In rugby league, how many tackles does a team have before handing over possession?
explanation: The rule started at four tackles in 1966 and moved to six in 1972; it is the structural difference that makes league so much faster than union.
hook: Six tackles then hand over — union has no such limit, which is why rucks matter.

question: Which Australian cyclist won the Tour de France in 2011?
explanation: He remains the only Australian to win it, taking the yellow jersey on the penultimate-day time trial after trailing throughout the final week.
hook: He took the lead with one day to go, in the time trial.

question: Which trophy do Australia and New Zealand contest in rugby union?
explanation: Donated by a New Zealand Governor-General in 1931, New Zealand has held it almost continuously since 2003; the Webb Ellis Cup is the World Cup itself.
hook: Australia last held it in 2002 — the longest drought in the fixture's history.

question: How many Olympic gold medals did Michael Phelps win in total?
explanation: He won twenty-eight medals in all across four Games, including eight golds in Beijing in 2008, the most at a single Olympics.
hook: Twenty-three golds, twenty-eight medals — more than most countries.

question: Which Australian cricketer captained the side to the 2003 and 2007 World Cup titles?
explanation: Steve Waugh won the 1999 final and Michael Clarke the 2015 title on home soil, giving Australia five World Cups in total by 2015.
hook: Waugh 1999, Ponting 2003 and 2007, Clarke 2015 — four captains, five titles with 1987.

question: Which stadium is known as the 'G' by Australians?
explanation: It seats about 100,000, hosted the 1956 Olympics and holds the traditional Boxing Day Test each year.
hook: Olympic stadium, Test venue and Grand Final home — all one ground.

question: In which sport is the Stanley Cup awarded?
explanation: First awarded in 1893, it is the oldest trophy competed for by professional athletes in North America, and every winning player's name is engraved on it.
hook: Every winner's name goes on the trophy itself, which is why it keeps getting taller.

question: Which Australian netball team competition is contested with New Zealand clubs' successor leagues?
explanation: The trans-Tasman ANZ Championship split in 2017 into Australia's Super Netball and New Zealand's ANZ Premiership; the Constellation Cup is the international series.
hook: The trans-Tasman league split in two in 2017 — one competition became two.

question: How many players are in a baseball team's batting lineup?
explanation: Nine fielders and nine batters, though the designated hitter rule allows one player to bat in place of the pitcher without fielding.
hook: Nine on the field, nine in the order, and the designated hitter breaks the symmetry.

question: Which Australian lit the cauldron and then won the 400 metres in Sydney?
explanation: The two moments were eleven days apart in the same stadium, and the race remains among the most watched broadcasts in Australian television history.
hook: She lit the flame and won the race in the same stadium, eleven days apart.

question: Which boxing weight division is contested at over 90.7 kilograms?
explanation: Cruiserweight sits just below at around 90.7 kilograms; heavyweight has no upper limit, which is why it produces the sport's biggest names.
hook: Heavyweight is the only division with no ceiling.

question: Which Australian AFL player kicked over 1,300 career goals?
explanation: He finished on 1,360, passing Gordon Coventry's long-standing record in 1999; Buddy Franklin became only the sixth player to reach a thousand.
hook: 1,360 goals, and only six players in history have even reached a thousand.

question: Which sport contests the Ryder Cup?
explanation: Contested biennially between the United States and Europe, it uses matchplay rather than strokeplay and pays no prize money to the players.
hook: No prize money, and it produces more pressure than any major.

question: How many gold medals did Australia win at the 2000 Sydney Olympics?
explanation: It was Australia's best Games at the time, with fifty-eight medals in total; Athens in 2004 delivered seventeen golds, the national record.
hook: Sydney sixteen, Athens seventeen — the away Games actually edged the home ones.

question: In cricket, what is it called when a bowler takes three wickets in three consecutive deliveries?
explanation: The term originated in cricket, where a bowler achieving it was presented with a hat; a maiden is an over with no runs scored.
hook: The hat was literal — a bowler who did it was given one.

question: Which Australian swimmer broke the 400m freestyle world record aged fifteen in 1971?
explanation: She held every world record from 100 to 1500 metres freestyle simultaneously, then retired at sixteen after winning three golds in Munich.
hook: She held every freestyle world record at once and retired at sixteen.

question: Which country won the first FIFA World Cup in 1930?
explanation: They hosted and beat Argentina 4-2 in the final; the two teams could not agree on a ball, so one was used in each half.
hook: They played the two halves with different balls because neither side would give way.

question: Which Australian rules football award is given to the best and fairest player of the season?
explanation: Umpires vote three, two and one after each match; the Norm Smith goes to the best on ground in the Grand Final and the Coleman to the leading goalkicker.
hook: Brownlow season, Norm Smith Grand Final, Coleman goals.

question: Which nation has won the most Olympic gold medals overall?
explanation: It has over a thousand summer golds, well clear of any other nation; the Soviet Union accumulated its total in far fewer Games before dissolving in 1991.
hook: The Soviet Union's rate per Games was higher — it simply ran out of Games.

question: Which Australian tennis player won the 1971 and 1980 Wimbledon women's singles titles?
explanation: Her 1980 win made her the first mother to take the title in sixty-six years; Margaret Court holds the all-time record of twenty-four grand slam singles titles.
hook: First mother to win Wimbledon in sixty-six years.

question: In athletics, how many events make up the decathlon?
explanation: The heptathlon has seven and the pentathlon five; the decathlon is contested over two days and its winner is traditionally called the world's greatest athlete.
hook: Deca ten, hepta seven, penta five — Greek numbers do the work.

question: Which Australian Formula One driver won the world championship in 1980?
explanation: Jack Brabham had won three titles in 1959, 1960 and 1966, the last in a car of his own construction, which no driver has done since.
hook: Brabham won a title in a car bearing his own name — still unique.

question: How long is an Olympic swimming pool?
explanation: Short-course world records are set in twenty-five metre pools and tracked separately, because extra turns make them significantly faster.
hook: Short-course records are faster because turns are quicker than swimming.

question: Which sport does the Sheffield Shield contest in Australia?
explanation: Contested between the states since 1892, it is the traditional pathway to Test selection and is named for an English earl who funded it.
hook: An English earl paid for the trophy that picks Australia's Test team.

question: Which country dominates the sport of table tennis at Olympic level?
explanation: China has won the overwhelming majority of Olympic table tennis golds since the sport's introduction in 1988, prompting rule changes intended to level the field.
hook: The rules have been changed several times specifically to make it less one-sided.

question: Which Australian won the 2019 and 2022 Wimbledon-era world number one ranking in women's tennis?
explanation: She won the French Open in 2019, Wimbledon in 2021 and the Australian Open in 2022, then retired at twenty-five while ranked number one.
hook: She retired at twenty-five as world number one, months after winning at home.

question: In rowing, what is the coxswain's role?
answer: To steer and direct the crew without rowing
distractors: To set the stroke rate from the bow
To row at the stern seat
To time the race from shore
explanation: The cox steers and calls the race while the stroke seat sets the rhythm; coxed and coxless events are scored as separate disciplines.
hook: The cox is the only person in the boat facing forwards.

question: Which Australian city hosted the 1982 Commonwealth Games?
explanation: Perth hosted in 1962, Melbourne in 2006 and the Gold Coast in 2018; the 1982 Games are remembered for the mechanical kangaroo mascot Matilda.
hook: The winking mechanical kangaroo is the most enduring thing about those Games.

question: How many strikes does it take to make a perfect game in ten-pin bowling?
explanation: Ten frames plus two bonus balls in the tenth produce a score of 300; the tenth frame allows three deliveries if the first two are strikes.
hook: Ten frames but twelve strikes — the last frame gives you two extra balls.

question: Which sport features the positions 'hooker', 'flanker' and 'fly-half'?
explanation: League shares the hooker but has no flanker and calls the fly-half a five-eighth, one of the code's clearest terminology differences.
hook: Fly-half in union, five-eighth in league — same job, different name.

question: Which Australian cricketer scored 380 in a Test innings against Zimbabwe in 2003?
explanation: It stood as the highest individual Test score for six months until Brian Lara made 400 not out against England in 2004.
hook: The record lasted six months before Lara took it back with 400.

question: In which sport is the Davis Cup contested?
explanation: Founded in 1900 as an international men's team competition; the women's equivalent is the Billie Jean King Cup, formerly the Fed Cup.
hook: Davis Cup men, Billie Jean King Cup women — same idea, two trophies.

question: Which Australian rugby league club has won the most premierships?
explanation: Souths have twenty-one titles, most from the early decades; St George's eleven consecutive premierships from 1956 to 1966 remain unmatched in Australian sport.
hook: Eleven premierships in a row by St George is the most dominant run in Australian sport.

question: How many players are on a volleyball team on court?
explanation: Beach volleyball uses two per side; the libero is a defensive specialist in indoor volleyball who wears a different coloured shirt and cannot attack.
hook: Six indoors, two on the sand, and one of the six wears a different shirt.

question: Which Australian bowler took a hat-trick in the 1994 Ashes at the MCG?
explanation: He dismissed Phil DeFreitas, Darren Gough and Devon Malcolm on Boxing Day; it was the first Ashes hat-trick by an Australian since Hugh Trumble in 1904.
hook: The first Australian Ashes hat-trick in ninety years.

question: Which Australian won an Olympic gold medal in speed skating in 2002?
explanation: He won the 1000m short track when every other finalist crashed on the last corner; Alisa Camplin won aerial skiing gold at the same Games days later.
hook: Australia's first Winter gold came from being the last man standing, literally.

question: Which cricketer has the highest individual score in a Test innings?
explanation: His 400 not out against England in Antigua in 2004 reclaimed the record he had lost to Matthew Hayden; he also holds the first-class record with 501 not out.
hook: He holds both the Test record with 400 and the first-class record with 501.

question: What is the record number of Melbourne Cups won by a single jockey?
explanation: Bobby Lewis managed it between 1902 and 1927 and Harry White between 1974 and 1979; Glen Boss won three consecutively aboard Makybe Diva.
hook: Four Cups each for two jockeys fifty years apart, and nobody has reached five.

question: In which year did Australia first compete at the Olympic Games as a nation rather than as individuals?
explanation: Edwin Flack competed in Athens in 1896 as an individual; from 1908 to 1912 Australia and New Zealand competed jointly as Australasia before separating.
hook: For two Games Australia and New Zealand competed as one team called Australasia.

question: Which Australian tennis player won all four grand slams in 1970?
explanation: She is one of only three women to complete a calendar-year grand slam in singles, alongside Maureen Connolly and Steffi Graf.
hook: Three women have done the calendar slam in singles, and she is the Australian.

question: Which sport's rules were codified at Rugby School and spread through the British Empire?
explanation: The story of William Webb Ellis picking up the ball in 1823 is almost certainly apocryphal, but the World Cup trophy is named after him regardless.
hook: The founding story is probably invented, and they named the World Cup after it anyway.

question: Which AFL club was formed by the 1996 merger of Fitzroy and the Brisbane Bears?
explanation: The Sydney Swans were not a merger but a relocation, having moved north from South Melbourne in 1982.
hook: Brisbane is a merger; Sydney is a relocation — two different things.

question: Which bowling tactic did England use against Australia in the 1932-33 Ashes series?
explanation: Fast bowling at the batsman's body with a packed leg-side field was designed to counter Bradman; it caused a diplomatic incident and the laws were later changed.
hook: A cricket tactic that became a genuine diplomatic incident between two governments.

question: Which incident in 1981 saw an Australian bowler roll the ball along the ground to deny New Zealand a six?
explanation: Trevor Chappell bowled underarm on his captain and brother Greg's instruction; it was legal at the time and was banned in one-day cricket immediately afterwards.
hook: It was entirely legal, which is precisely why the law was changed within days.

question: Which Australian won consecutive Olympic gold medals in the 400m freestyle in 2000 and 2004?
explanation: Grant Hackett won the 1500m at both Games, and Kieren Perkins had won that event in 1992 and 1996 — four consecutive Olympic 1500m titles for Australia.
hook: Perkins then Hackett gave Australia four straight Olympic 1500m titles.

question: Which country won the first Rugby World Cup in 1987?
explanation: Australia won in 1991 and 1999, South Africa in 1995, 2007, 2019 and 2023; South Africa was excluded from the first two tournaments over apartheid.
hook: South Africa missed the first two World Cups entirely and has since won four.

question: Which Australian athlete won gold in the 1500m at the 1960 Rome Olympics?
explanation: He won by a record margin in world-record time and was never beaten over the mile or 1500m in his career; Percy Cerutty was his coach.
hook: Never beaten over the mile or 1500m, ever, in his entire career.

question: Which golf tournament is played at the same course every year?
explanation: Augusta National has hosted it since 1934; the other three majors rotate venues, and the Open uses a fixed pool of links courses.
hook: The only major with a permanent home.

question: What is the highest number of Brownlow Medals won by any single player?
explanation: Haydn Bunton Senior, Dick Reynolds, Bob Skilton and Ian Stewart each won three; no player has managed a fourth in the medal's century of history.
hook: Four players on three each, and nobody has ever won a fourth.

question: Which Australian beat world record holder Matt Biondi in the 1988 200m freestyle?
explanation: Swimming from lane six, he drafted off Biondi's wash for most of the race and won in world record time in Seoul.
hook: He beat the world record holder by surfing his wash from the next lane.

question: Which Australian boxer held a world title and was known as 'The Man'?
explanation: He won world titles in three weight divisions; Lionel Rose was the first Indigenous Australian world champion, taking the bantamweight title in 1968.
hook: Lionel Rose was first, in 1968, and became Australian of the Year for it.

question: In cricket, what is the fielding position directly behind the wicketkeeper called?
explanation: It is rarely used in modern cricket now that keepers reliably stop the ball; fine leg and third man are behind square on either side.
hook: A position so obsolete that seeing one used is itself the news.

question: Which Australian won the Wimbledon men's singles in 1987?
explanation: He climbed into the players' box to reach his family after beating Ivan Lendl, starting a tradition later copied by many champions.
hook: He invented the climb into the players' box after winning.

question: How many countries have hosted the Summer Olympics more than twice?
explanation: The United States has hosted four times and will host a fifth in 2028; the United Kingdom has hosted three, all in London.
hook: London is the only city to host three times.

question: Which Australian sprinter set a 200m world record in 1968 that stood for decades in Australian terms?
explanation: His 20.06 seconds in Mexico City remains the Australian record; he wore a human rights badge on the podium in support of Smith and Carlos and was ostracised afterwards.
hook: The third man on that famous podium was Australian, and it cost him his career.

question: Which sport's world governing body is the FIA?
explanation: The Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile governs Formula One and rallying; cycling's body is the UCI, athletics' is World Athletics and sailing's is World Sailing.
hook: FIA cars, UCI bikes, FINA swimming — the acronyms are all French in origin.

question: Which Australian cricketer captained the side in the 2018 ball-tampering incident in South Africa?
explanation: He and David Warner received twelve-month bans and Cameron Bancroft nine months; Tim Paine took over the captaincy immediately afterwards.
hook: Two twelve-month bans and a captaincy change inside a week.

question: Which Australian yacht race runs from Sydney on Boxing Day?
explanation: Run since 1945 over 628 nautical miles, the 1998 race killed six sailors when a violent storm struck the fleet in Bass Strait.
hook: The 1998 race killed six sailors and rewrote offshore safety rules worldwide.

question: Which Australian was the first woman to win an Olympic marathon medal for the country?
explanation: She took silver in Seoul in 1988 competing as Lisa Martin; Kerryn McCann won Commonwealth Games marathon golds in 2002 and 2006.
hook: Silver in Seoul 1988 — Australia's only Olympic marathon medal by a woman.

question: In rugby league, what is the Dally M Medal awarded for?
answer: The best player of the NRL season
distractors: The best forward of the season
explanation: Named for Dally Messenger, an early code-switching star; the Clive Churchill Medal goes to the best player in the grand final.
hook: Dally M for the season, Clive Churchill for the grand final.

question: Which Australian won an Olympic gold medal in the 1500m freestyle in 1992 and 1996?
explanation: His 1996 win came from lane eight after barely qualifying for the final, one of the most improbable title defences in Olympic swimming.
hook: He defended the title from lane eight after scraping into the final.

question: Which country introduced the modern marathon distance of 42.195 kilometres?
explanation: The 1908 London Olympics extended the course so it could start at Windsor Castle and finish before the royal box; the distance was standardised in 1921.
hook: The odd distance exists so the race could finish in front of the royal box.

question: Which Australian racehorse won thirty-three consecutive races between 2015 and 2019?
explanation: She won four Cox Plates in a row; Black Caviar retired unbeaten after twenty-five starts, all at sprint distances.
hook: Thirty-three in a row for Winx, twenty-five unbeaten for Black Caviar.

question: Which sport uses the terms 'peloton', 'domestique' and 'echelon'?
explanation: A domestique sacrifices their own result to support the team leader; an echelon is a diagonal formation used to shelter from crosswinds.
hook: The domestique is a rider paid to lose so someone else can win.

question: Which Australian AFL team entered the competition in 2012 as its eighteenth club?
explanation: The Gold Coast Suns entered in 2011 as the seventeenth, and the two expansion clubs received significant draft concessions to build lists from scratch.
hook: Gold Coast 2011, GWS 2012 — the last two clubs added.

question: In cricket, what does a bowler's economy rate measure?
explanation: Average is runs per wicket and strike rate is balls per wicket; economy matters most in limited-overs cricket where containment can outweigh wicket-taking.
hook: Economy per over, average per wicket, strike rate in balls.

question: Which Australian won Olympic gold in the men's 100m butterfly in 1984?
explanation: He came from fifth at the turn to beat world record holder Michael Gross in Los Angeles, taking almost two seconds off his personal best.
hook: He improved his own best by nearly two seconds to win — in a final.

question: Which nation won the most medals at the 2020 Tokyo Paralympic Games?
explanation: China has topped the Paralympic medal table at every Summer Games since 2004; Australia finished eighth in Tokyo with eighty medals.
hook: China has topped the Paralympic table at every Games since Athens.

question: Which Australian golfer led the 1996 US Masters by six shots and lost?
explanation: He shot 78 in the final round while Nick Faldo shot 67, a collapse that remains one of golf's most discussed final days.
hook: Six shots up on Sunday morning, five behind by Sunday night.

question: Which Australian sprinter won four Commonwealth Games gold medals in the 1970s?
explanation: She won three Olympic silvers, all behind East German sprinters later implicated in state doping programmes; Betty Cuthbert won four Olympic golds in the 1950s and 1960s.
hook: Three Olympic silvers, all behind athletes from a state doping programme.

question: Which sport contests the Webb Ellis Cup?
explanation: Rugby league's world championship trophy is the Paul Barrière Trophy; Australia has won the league world cup twelve times, more than any other nation in any code.
hook: Australia has twelve rugby league world cups — the most dominant record in any team sport.

question: Which Australian cricket ground hosts the traditional Boxing Day Test?
explanation: The SCG traditionally holds the New Year Test that follows; crowds at the MCG on the first day regularly exceed 80,000.
hook: Boxing Day in Melbourne, New Year in Sydney — the summer's fixed points.

question: Which country has won the most Olympic medals in sailing?
explanation: Britain has topped the Olympic sailing medal table at several recent Games; Australia's most successful sailors include Tom Burton and the 470 crews.
hook: The island nation that invented yacht racing still leads the medal table.

question: In tennis, what is the tiebreak score required to win a standard set tiebreak?
answer: Seven points with a margin of two
distractors: Six points with a margin of two
Ten points with a margin of two
explanation: Final-set rules varied for decades until the four slams standardised on a ten-point tiebreak at six games all in 2022.
hook: The four slams only agreed on a single final-set rule in 2022.

question: Which Australian won the Formula One world championship in 1959, 1960 and 1966?
explanation: His 1966 title came in a car built by his own team, making him the only driver ever to win a world championship in a car bearing his own name.
hook: The only champion to beat everyone in a car with his own name on it.

question: Which cricket format was introduced in England in 2003 and revolutionised the sport commercially?
explanation: Designed to fit an evening, it produced the Indian Premier League in 2008, now the wealthiest cricket competition in the world by a wide margin.
hook: Invented to fill English evenings, and it made Indian cricket the richest in the world.

question: Who was the first Indigenous Australian to represent the country in any sport?
explanation: She played cricket for Australia in 1958; Lionel Rose became world bantamweight boxing champion in 1968 and was named Australian of the Year for it.
hook: A fast bowler in 1958, a decade before Lionel Rose won his world title.

question: Which Australian AFL competition began a national women's league in 2017?
explanation: AFLW launched in 2017 with eight clubs; the Women's Big Bash League in cricket had begun in 2015 and the W-League in soccer in 2008.
hook: W-League 2008, WBBL 2015, AFLW 2017 — the order Australian women's leagues arrived.

question: Which nation won the inaugural Women's Cricket World Cup in 1973?
explanation: It was held two years before the first men's tournament; Australia has since won the competition more times than any other nation.
hook: The women's World Cup predates the men's by two years.

question: Which Australian holds the record for the most Test wickets by a spin bowler after Muttiah Muralitharan?
explanation: Muralitharan finished with 800 and Warne 708; Nathan Lyon has become Australia's most successful off-spinner and passed 500.
hook: 800 for Murali, 708 for Warne, and Lyon past 500 — the spin ladder.

question: In which sport did Australia win its first Olympic gold medal at a Winter Games?
explanation: Steven Bradbury's 2002 win in the 1000m came days before Alisa Camplin's aerial skiing gold at the same Games.
hook: Two Australian Winter golds within a week, after a century of none.

question: Which international football tournament did Australia first qualify for in 1974 before a thirty-two-year absence?
explanation: The Socceroos next qualified in 2006 after beating Uruguay on penalties, and Australia moved from the Oceania to the Asian confederation the same year.
hook: One appearance in 1974, then nothing until a penalty shootout in 2005.

question: Which Australian tennis player won the US Open in 1997 and 1998?
explanation: Lleyton Hewitt won the US Open in 2001 and Wimbledon in 2002, and was the youngest man to reach world number one at twenty.
hook: Rafter took two US Opens; Hewitt took the third Australian one in 2001.

question: Which Australian sports institution was founded in Canberra in 1981 after a poor Olympic showing?
explanation: Australia won no gold at the 1976 Montreal Games, prompting its creation; the model has since been copied by Britain, Canada and others.
hook: Zero golds in Montreal produced the institute that fixed it.

question: How many players are on a cricket team on the field?
explanation: Eleven per side, with a twelfth man permitted to field as a substitute but not to bat, bowl or keep wicket in the traditional laws.
hook: The twelfth man can field and carry drinks, and nothing else.

question: Which Australian won the Wimbledon women's doubles and reached the 2011 US Open final?
explanation: She won the 2011 US Open singles title, beating Serena Williams in straight sets, and was a former doubles world number one.
hook: She beat Serena Williams in a US Open final in straight sets.

question: In which sport do teams compete for the Sheffield Shield's one-day equivalent?
explanation: The domestic one-day competition has run under many sponsor names since 1969; the Shield remains the four-day first-class competition.
hook: Shield for the long form, and the one-day cup keeps changing its name.

question: Which Australian won an Olympic gold medal in the women's 400m freestyle in 2021?
explanation: She beat Katie Ledecky, who had been unbeaten in major finals over the distance for years; her coach's reaction became one of the Games' defining images.
hook: Her coach's celebration got more airtime than the race.

question: Which Australian rules football rule change of 1973 introduced the centre square?
distractors: The out of bounds on the full rule
explanation: It limited the number of players allowed inside the square at a centre bounce to four per team, breaking up the congestion of unrestricted ruck contests.
hook: Four players a side inside the square — the first serious attempt to stop congestion.
